title: From objects to landmarks: the function of visual location information in spatial navigation

findings.antecedent: Object uniqueness and informative features within an environment
findings.consequent: Likelihood of being used as a landmark
findings.quote: the more unique an object is within an environment, and the more informative its features are, the more likely it is that it will be used as a landmark

findings.antecedent: Presence of stable objects in the environment
findings.consequent: Navigational performance
findings.quote: the presence of stable objects in the environment can significantly improve navigational performance.

findings.antecedent: Animal observes that the spatial location of an object has moved over time
findings.consequent: Object's influence on hippocampal place cell activity
findings.quote: an object's influence on hippocampal place cell activity is lost when the animal observes that the spatial location of the object has moved over time

findings.antecedent: Objects rated by participants as larger and less 'portable' (more stable)
findings.consequent: Activity within the parahippocampal gyrus
findings.quote: Objects that were rated by participants as larger and less 'portable' elicited an increase in activity within the parahippocampal gyrus.

findings.antecedent: Spatial judgments made with reference to stable environmental objects (compared to unstable objects)
findings.consequent: Activity in navigationally relevant medial parietal and temporal brain regions (including hippocampus)
findings.quote: making spatial judgments with reference to stable environmental objects... elicit greater activity in navigationally relevant medial parietal and temporal brain regions, including the hippocampus

findings.antecedent: Objects located at navigational decision points (e.g., a T-intersection)
findings.consequent: Importance for verbal route descriptions
findings.quote: objects that occupy locations at which a navigational decision has to be made... are more important for verbal route descriptions

findings.antecedent: Objects located at decision points
findings.consequent: Memory/recognition
findings.quote: objects at decision points are better remembered than those at non-decision points

findings.antecedent: Objects at decision points
findings.consequent: Activity in the left and right parahippocampal gyri
findings.quote: Functional MRI data showed increased activity in the left and right parahippocampal gyri for objects at decision points relative to those at non-decision points.

findings.antecedent: Objects at decision points (remembered or forgotten)
findings.consequent: Automatic coding of navigational relevance (reflected in parahippocampal activity)
findings.quote: decision point related increases in parahippocampal activity were observed for remembered as well as for forgotten objects, suggesting that the coding of navigational relevance is an automatic process that does not require explicit memory.

findings.antecedent: Buildings at decision points (in a real-world setting, especially in less familiar campus parts)
findings.consequent: Recognition and parahippocampal activity
findings.quote: buildings at decision points were more readily recognized than buildings at non-decision points. Subsequent fMRI revealed increased parahippocampal activity for pictures of buildings that had appeared at decision points than for those at non-decision points, but only for buildings that occupied less familiar parts of the campus.

findings.antecedent: Damage to the parahippocampal gyrus
findings.consequent: Landmark agnosia, impaired recognition of salient environmental landmarks, and significant way-finding deficits
findings.quote: Damage to the parahippocampal gyrus has been found to cause a form of topographical disorientation termed 'landmark agnosia' in which the patient is selectively impaired in recognizing salient environmental landmarks, and thus exhibits significant way-finding deficits

findings.antecedent: Objects with stronger perceptual features (when in conflict with spatial positioning)
findings.consequent: Object recognition speed
findings.quote: when these two cues are placed in conflict, objects with stronger perceptual features were later recognized faster irrespective of their spatial positioning.

findings.antecedent: Spatial positioning of objects
findings.consequent: Determination of whether objects are included in direction giving and map drawing
findings.quote: it was spatial positioning that determined whether objects were included in direction giving and map drawing.

findings.antecedent: Objects serving as beacons (compared to associative cues)
findings.consequent: Route learning efficiency
findings.quote: When objects served as beacons, route learning was more efficient than when they acted as associative cues.

findings.antecedent: Beacon-based route learning
findings.consequent: Enduring representation of route information and directional information
findings.quote: beacon-based route learning led to a less enduring representation of route information and a poorer representation of directional information.

findings.antecedent: Availability of beacon-like cues during learning
findings.consequent: Learning of other spatial information
findings.quote: the availability of beacon-like cues during learning is enough to block or overshadow the learning of other spatial information

findings.antecedent: Damage to the dorsal striatum (in rats)
findings.consequent: Ability to use beacon cues in spatial navigation tasks
findings.quote: rats with damage to the dorsal striatum are unable to use beacon cues in spatial navigation tasks

findings.antecedent: Beacon-based navigation
findings.consequent: Metabolic activity in the caudate nucleus
findings.quote: metabolic activity associated with beacon-based navigation is associated with increased activity in the caudate nucleus

findings.antecedent: Goal location indicated by a beacon cue (in humans)
findings.consequent: Striatal activity
findings.quote: observed striatal activity during navigation tasks where the goal location was indicated by a beacon cue

findings.antecedent: Heading disorientation (due to lesions in posterior-medial brain regions like retrosplenial cortex)
findings.consequent: Difficulty using visual environmental information for heading and significant navigational impairments
findings.quote: Patients with a condition known as 'heading disorientation' have difficulty using visual environmental information to determine their current heading

findings.antecedent: Animal's heading during navigation
findings.consequent: Head-direction cell firing activity
findings.quote: Head-direction cells exhibit firing activity that is tied to an animal's heading during navigation

findings.antecedent: Rotation of salient objects around an arena
findings.consequent: Similar rotations in the preferred firing direction of head-direction cells
findings.quote: Rotation of salient objects around an arena causes similar rotations in the preferred firing direction of head-direction cells

findings.antecedent: Environmental visual cues (when in artificial conflict with idiothetic information)
findings.consequent: Head-direction cell firing consistency
findings.quote: head-direction cells fire more consistently in response to environmental visual cues when visual and idiothetic information is artificially placed in conflict

findings.antecedent: Discrete visual cues (compared to geometric cues)
findings.consequent: Influence on head direction cells and computation of heading vectors
findings.quote: head-direction cells are strongly influenced by discrete visual cues, whereas geometric cues only provide a weak influence for the computation of heading vectors

findings.antecedent: Objects corresponding to the same heading direction (relative to objects corresponding to different directions)
findings.consequent: Neural activity in the medial parietal cortex
findings.quote: Neural activity in the medial parietal cortex was significantly reduced for objects that corresponded to the same heading direction relative to objects that corresponded to different directions, indicating neural adaptation as a function of heading within this brain area.

findings.antecedent: Routes containing salient objects as landmarks (compared to routes without such objects)
findings.consequent: Ability to learn a novel route
findings.quote: our ability to learn a novel route between two locations is significantly better for routes that contain salient objects that act as landmarks

findings.antecedent: New combination of buildings at an intersection associated with the same directional movement during training
findings.consequent: Navigational performance
findings.quote: participants' performance was as good as in the trained condition if the new combination of buildings at an intersection was associated with the same directional movement during training

findings.antecedent: New combination of buildings at an intersection associated with a direction that conflicted with that established during training
findings.consequent: Navigational performance
findings.quote: Conversely, performance was poorer if the new combination of buildings at an intersection contained buildings associated with a direction that conflicted with that established during training.

findings.antecedent: Objects at decision points along a path
findings.consequent: Parahippocampal activity
findings.quote: objects at decision points along a path elicit increased parahippocampal activity relative to objects at non-decision points

findings.antecedent: Number of contextual associations elicited by a visual scene
findings.consequent: Parahippocampal cortex activity
findings.quote: activity in the parahippocampal cortex can be modulated by the number of contextual associations that are elicited by a visual scene

findings.antecedent: Increased angular disparity between the presented view and the studied view of object-arrays
findings.consequent: Spatial recognition performance for remembered object-arrays
findings.quote: spatial recognition performance for remembered object-arrays decreased in a linear fashion as the angular disparity between the presented view and the studied view increased

findings.antecedent: Explicitly available environmental reference frames
findings.consequent: Organization of spatial information representation
findings.quote: the representation of spatial information can also be organized around environmental reference frames when these are explicitly available

findings.antecedent: Imagined orientation aligned with a salient frame of reference (compared to misaligned orientations)
findings.consequent: Spatial judgments for a learned object-array
findings.quote: spatial judgments for a learned object-array is significantly better when made from an imagined orientation that is aligned with a salient frame of reference than when made from orientations that are misaligned

findings.antecedent: Geometric cues (compared to featural cues)
findings.consequent: Use for reorientation (in rats)
findings.quote: rats preferentially use geometric cues over featural cues for reorientation.

findings.antecedent: Disorientation in a rectangular room (even with available featural cues)
findings.consequent: Rotational errors (in young children, indicating preferential use of geometry)
findings.quote: Young children... display similar rotational errors after disorientation when searching for a toy within a rectangular room, even when featural cues are available to distinguish the two corners

findings.antecedent: Spatial learning based on boundary information (compared to discrete proximal landmarks)
findings.consequent: Distinct sets of behavioral and neural processes
findings.quote: spatial learning based upon boundary information and discrete proximal landmarks involve two distinct sets of behavioral and neural processes

findings.antecedent: Boundary-related target objects
findings.consequent: Hippocampal activation
findings.quote: Learning trials for boundary-related target objects were associated with increased hippocampal activation

findings.antecedent: Discrete proximal objects
findings.consequent: Striatal activity
findings.quote: trials concerning discrete proximal objects were associated with increased striatal activity

findings.antecedent: Imagining empty visual scenes with a 'wall-like' object (compared to without the object)
findings.consequent: Hippocampal activity
findings.quote: imagining empty visual scenes with a discrete, 'wall-like' object... resulted in an increase in hippocampal activity compared with imagining a scene without the object

findings.antecedent: Increased number of 'wall-like' objects in an imagined scene
findings.consequent: Hippocampal activity (reflecting boundary information)
findings.quote: Increasing the number of wall-like objects in the imagined scene resulted in an increase in the amount of hippocampal activity, again supporting the notion that hippocampal activity reflects, at least to some extent, the amount of boundary information present in an environment.

findings.antecedent: Changes to the geometric properties of an environment (e.g., expansion of rectangular environments)
findings.consequent: Place cell firing (parametric stretching and reforming of place fields)
findings.quote: changes to the geometric properties of an environment might result in relative changes in place cell firing. Expansion of rectangular environments resulted in parametric stretching and reforming of place fields.

findings.antecedent: Shape of environmental boundaries
findings.consequent: Neuronal firing patterns in brain regions (subiculum and medial entorhinal cortex)
findings.quote: the shape of environmental boundaries modulates the neuronal firing patterns in these brain regions
